chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from a Sheikh from the people of Kufa, from one of our companions, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him), who said:

I asked him, saying, 'May I be sacrificed for you! A man entered the house of a man, and a dog leaped upon him in the house and injured him.' So he (peace be upon him) said: 'If he was invited, then upon the people of the house is the compensation for the scratch; and if he was notching (injury); and if he was not invited, so he entered (of his own accord), then there is nothing upon them.'
ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic legal ruling on a dog injuring a guest in a house?
ai.summary: This hadith from al-Kafi delineates the principle of *daman* (financial liability) for animal injuries, distinguishing between an invited guest, where the homeowners bear the cost of minor wounds (*khashm*), and an uninvited entrant, who bears no compensation. It reflects the Shia juristic emphasis on implied hospitality and the degree of control exerted by the homeowner over their property, a nuance critical in deriving rulings on animal liability in *fiqh*.

en.hubeali: Ali Bin Ibrahim, from his father, from Sheykh from the people of Al Kufa, from one of our companions,

(The narrator) says, ‘I asked Abu Abdullah<sup>asws</sup> saying, ‘May I be sacrificed for you<sup>asws</sup>! A man enters a house of a man, so a dog leaps upon him in the house, so it injures him’. So he<sup>asws</sup> said: ‘If he was invited, so it is upon the people of the house, the compensation of the scratch; and if he was not invited, so he entered (of his own accord), so there is nothing upon them’.
